p.src: Now Song Jiang, wishing to avoid a cup of wine, had gone to relieve himself. As he came back beneath the gallery, he stepped on the handle of a fire shovel, provoking the man into such a rage that he sprang up and made to strike him. Chai Jin hurried out after them and happened to call him Magistrate's Clerk Song, thereby revealing his name. When the burly fellow heard that this was Song Jiang, he fell to his knees and refused to rise, saying, “This humble man had eyes but failed to recognize Mount Tai! In my rashness I offended you, elder brother. I beg you to forgive me.” Song Jiang helped the man to his feet and asked, “Who are you, sir? What is your honorable name?” Pointing to him, Chai Jin said, “This man is a native of Qinghe County. His surname is Wu, his given name Song, and he is the second son. He has been here for a year now.” Song Jiang said, “I have often heard the name of Second Brother Wu spoken of throughout the rivers and lakes. I never expected to meet you here today. What great good fortune!”

p.src: Chai Jin said, “For heroes to meet by chance is truly a rare event. Please sit together at one table and talk.”

p.src: Song Jiang was delighted. Taking Wu Song by the hand, he led him to the banquet in the rear hall and called Song Qing over to meet him. Chai Jin invited Wu Song to take a seat. Song Jiang promptly urged him to sit with them in the place of honor. Wu Song would not hear of it. After much polite yielding, he finally took the third seat. Chai Jin ordered fresh cups and dishes to be laid out and urged the three men to drink their fill. As Song Jiang studied Wu Song by lamplight, he saw that the man was indeed a true hero. p.src: His frame was imposing, his countenance noble. His two eyes flashed like cold stars; his arched brows seemed brushed with lacquer. His chest was broad and mighty, bearing the awe of one whom ten thousand men could not withstand; His speech was lofty and bold, voicing an ambition that soared a thousand fathoms into the clouds. Proud of heart and great in courage, he was like a heaven-shaking lion descending from the clouds; Strong of bone and sinew, he was like an earth-shaking pixiu arriving before the seat. He seemed a demon-subduing lord descended from heaven, truly a god of fate walking among men.

His speech was lofty and bold, voicing an ambition that soared a thousand fathoms into the clouds.

Strong of bone and sinew, he was like an earth-shaking pixiu arriving before the seat.
He seemed a demon-subduing lord descended from heaven, truly a god of fate walking among men.

p.src: As Song Jiang regarded Wu Song’s magnificent bearing beneath the lamp, he was greatly pleased and asked him, “Second Brother, what brought you here?” Wu Song replied, “In Qinghe County I once became drunk and quarreled with a local confidential clerk. Anger seized me, and with a single blow I knocked the wretch senseless. I thought I had killed him, so I fled straight here and sought refuge with His Honor, hiding from disaster. I have now been here for more than a year. Later I learned that the fellow had not died after all, but had been revived. I was just preparing to return home and seek out my elder brother, but then I contracted malaria and was unable to set out. Just now a chill had come upon me, and I was warming myself by the fire beneath the gallery. When you stepped on the shovel handle, elder brother, the shock made me break out in a cold sweat, and now I feel the illness has left me.” Song Jiang was delighted to hear this. That night they drank until the third watch. When the drinking ended, Song Jiang kept Wu Song with him, lodging together beneath the western pavilion. The next morning Chai Jin laid out a banquet, slaughtering sheep and pigs to entertain Song Jiang; but there is no need to dwell on that.

p.src: Several days later, Song Jiang took out some silver to have clothes made for Wu Song. When Chai Jin learned of it, he would not permit Song Jiang to spend his money. He brought out a chest of satin, damask, and silk, and since he had tailors among his retainers, ordered well-fitting clothes made for all three men.

p.src: But why, you may ask, did Chai Jin not like Wu Song? When Wu Song first came seeking refuge with Chai Jin, he too had been welcomed and entertained in the customary manner. But afterward, whenever he got drunk at the manor, his temper was so fierce that if the servants failed him in the slightest, he would try to beat them with his fists. Thus, among all the servants in the manor, not one had a good word to say for him. They all disliked him and went before Chai Jin with long accounts of his faults. Though Chai Jin did not drive him away, he began to treat him with less regard. Fortunately, Song Jiang took him along every day and kept him company over wine, and Wu Song’s former illness never returned.

p.src: After spending more than ten days in Song Jiang’s company, Wu Song grew homesick and wished to return to Qinghe County to visit his elder brother. Both Chai Jin and Song Jiang urged him to stay a while longer. Wu Song said, “I have had no news from my elder brother for a long time, and so I wish to go and see him.” Song Jiang said, “If you truly must go, Second Brother, I dare not press you to remain. When you have leisure, come back and spend some time with us again.” Wu Song thanked Song Jiang. Chai Jin brought out some gold and silver to give Wu Song, who thanked him, saying, “I have truly imposed upon Your Honor far too much.” Wu Song tied up his bundle, secured his quarterstaff, and prepared to depart. Chai Jin once more prepared food and wine for his journey. Wu Song put on a newly padded jacket of red silk and a white Fanyang felt hat, slung his bundle over his back, took up his staff, bade them farewell, and set off. Song Jiang said, “Worthy brother, wait a moment.” He returned to his room, took some silver, and hurried out to the manor gate, saying, “I shall accompany you part of the way.” Song Jiang and his younger brother Song Qing set out to see Wu Song off. After Wu Song had taken leave of His Honor Chai, Song Jiang also said, “Your Honor, I shall bid you farewell for now and return shortly.”

p.src: The three left Chai Jin’s eastern manor and walked some five or seven li. Then Wu Song took his leave, saying, “Honored brothers, you have come far enough. Please turn back. His Honor Chai must surely be waiting especially for you.” Song Jiang said, “What harm is there in going a few steps farther?” Chatting idly along the road, they unwittingly covered another two or three li. Wu Song caught hold of Song Jiang and said, “Honored brother, there is no need to see me any farther. As the saying goes, ‘Though you escort a friend a thousand li, in the end you must part.’” Song Jiang pointed ahead and said, “Allow me to go just a little farther. There is a little wineshop over there on the highway. Let us drink three cups before we part.”

p.src: The three entered the wineshop. Song Jiang took the seat of honor; Wu Song leaned his quarterstaff nearby and sat at the lower end; Song Qing sat crosswise at the side. They called for the wine attendant to bring wine and bought assorted dishes, fruit, and vegetables, all of which were carried over and arranged on the table. After the three had drunk several cups, the red sun was already sinking level with the west. Wu Song said, “It is growing late. If elder brother does not disdain this Second Wu, then let me make four obeisances here and acknowledge you as my sworn elder brother.” Song Jiang was overjoyed. Wu Song bowed his head to the ground four times. Song Jiang then told Song Qing to take out a ten-tael ingot of silver and present it to Wu Song. Wu Song would not accept it, saying, “Elder brother, you need it for your own traveling expenses while away from home.” Song Jiang said, “Worthy brother, do not concern yourself. If you refuse it, I shall no longer acknowledge you as my brother.” Wu Song had no choice but to bow and accept it, placing it in his money pouch. Song Jiang took out some pieces of silver and paid for the wine. Wu Song picked up his quarterstaff, and the three went out before the wineshop to say farewell. Shedding tears, Wu Song bowed farewell and went on his way alone.

p.src: Song Jiang and Song Qing stood before the wineshop until Wu Song had vanished from sight; only then did they turn back. Before they had gone five li, they saw His Honor Chai riding toward them, with two riderless horses led behind him. Song Jiang was delighted to see him, and together they mounted the horses and returned to the manor. After dismounting, they were invited into the rear hall to drink. From then on, Song Jiang and his brother remained at His Honor Chai’s manor.

p.src: Now the tale divides into two paths. Let us speak only of Wu Song. After parting from Song Jiang, he lodged at an inn that evening. Early the next morning, he rose, had the fire lit, ate his meal, paid for his room, secured his bundle, took up his quarterstaff, and set out on the road, thinking, “Throughout the rivers and lakes I had only heard men speak of Song Gongming, the ‘Timely Rain,’ but his fame is indeed no empty thing. To have made a brother such as this—my journey has not been in vain!”

p.src: After traveling for several days, Wu Song reached the district of Yanggu County. The county seat was still a long way off. Around noon that day, hungry and thirsty from walking, he saw an inn ahead with a banner hanging before its door. Five words were written upon it: “Three Bowls and You Cannot Cross the Ridge.”

u.src: After traveling for several days, Wu Song reached the district of Yanggu County.
The county seat was still a long way off.
Around noon that day, hungry and thirsty from walking, he saw an inn ahead with a banner hanging before its door. Five words were written upon it: “Three Bowls and You Cannot Cross the Ridge.”

p.src: Wu Song went inside and sat down. Leaning his quarterstaff against the wall, he called, “Innkeeper, bring me wine at once!” The innkeeper set three bowls, a pair of chopsticks, and a dish of hot food before Wu Song, then filled one bowl to the brim with wine. Wu Song lifted the bowl and drained it at a draught. “This wine has a mighty kick! Innkeeper, bring me something filling to go with it.” The innkeeper said, “I have only cooked beef.” Wu Song said, “That will do. Cut me two or three catties to eat with the wine.” The innkeeper went inside, cut two catties of cooked beef, piled it upon a large platter, and set it before Wu Song; then he poured him another bowl of wine. Wu Song drank it and said, “Fine wine!” The innkeeper poured him one more bowl. But once Wu Song had drunk exactly three bowls, the innkeeper poured no more. Wu Song rapped on the table and called, “Innkeeper, why are you not pouring more wine?” The innkeeper replied, “If you want more meat, sir, I will bring it.” Wu Song said, “I want wine as well, and cut me some more meat.” The innkeeper said, “I can cut more meat for you, sir, but I shall bring no more wine.” Wu Song said, “That is a strange business!” Then he asked the innkeeper, “Why will you not sell me any more wine?” The innkeeper said, “Sir, you must have seen what is plainly written on the banner outside my door: ‘Three Bowls and You Cannot Cross the Ridge.’”

p.src: Wu Song asked, “What do you mean by ‘Three Bowls and You Cannot Cross the Ridge’?”

u.src: Wu Song asked, “What do you mean by ‘Three Bowls and You Cannot Cross the Ridge’?”

p.src: The innkeeper said, “Though ours is only country wine, its flavor surpasses even well-aged liquor. Any traveler who comes to my inn and drinks three bowls becomes drunk and cannot cross the ridge ahead. That is why we call it ‘Three Bowls and You Cannot Cross the Ridge.’ Travelers passing this way drink only three bowls and ask for no more.” Wu Song laughed. “So that is the reason. But I have drunk three bowls. Why am I not drunk?” The innkeeper said, “This wine of mine is called ‘Fragrance Through the Jar,’ and also ‘Down Outside the Door.’ At first it tastes rich and mellow, but in a little while it lays you flat.” Wu Song said, “Stop talking nonsense! Do you think I will not pay you? Pour me three more bowls!” Seeing that Wu Song was entirely unaffected, the innkeeper poured him three more bowls. Wu Song drank them and said, “Truly excellent wine! Innkeeper, for every bowl I drink, I shall pay you for a bowl. Just keep pouring.” The innkeeper said, “Sir, do not insist on drinking. This wine truly fells a man, and no medicine can cure him.” Wu Song said, “Stop your damned nonsense! Even if you had put knockout drops in it, I have a nose and would know.” Unable to withstand his angry demands, the innkeeper poured him three more bowls in succession. Wu Song said, “Bring me another two catties of meat as well.” The innkeeper cut another two catties of cooked beef and poured three more bowls of wine. Wu Song had acquired a taste for it and kept demanding more. Taking some small pieces of silver from his person, he called, “Innkeeper, come and look at my silver. Is it enough to pay for the wine and meat?” The innkeeper looked and said, “More than enough. I shall have to give you some change.” Wu Song said, “I want no change. Just bring the wine and pour.” The innkeeper said, “Sir, if you still want to drink, there are another five or six bowls left! I fear you will not be able to finish them.” Wu Song said, “Even if there are five or six bowls more, pour out every last one and bring them here.” The innkeeper said, “You are such a great tall fellow—if you fall down drunk, how could I possibly hold you up?” Wu Song replied, “If I needed you to hold me up, I would be no true man.” Still the innkeeper refused to pour the wine. Wu Song grew angry. “It is not as though I were drinking your wine for nothing! Do not provoke my temper, or I shall smash everything in your house to pieces! I shall turn this damned inn of yours upside down!” The innkeeper said to himself, “The brute is drunk; best not provoke him.” So he poured another six bowls, which Wu Song drank. Having drunk fifteen bowls altogether, Wu Song snatched up his quarterstaff, rose, and said, “And I am still not drunk!” Stepping out through the door, he laughed and said, “So much for ‘Three Bowls and You Cannot Cross the Ridge’!” With his quarterstaff in hand, he set off.

p.src: Wu Song stopped and asked, “Why are you calling me? I have not shortchanged you for the wine, so what do you want with me?” The innkeeper called, “I mean you well. Come back inside and look at the copy of the authorities’ proclamation.”

p.src: Wu Song asked, “What proclamation?”

u.src: Wu Song asked, “What proclamation?”

p.src: The innkeeper said, “There is now a great white-fronted, glaring-eyed tiger on Jingyang Ridge. It comes out late in the day to attack people and has already taken the lives of twenty or thirty strong men. The authorities have ordered the hunters, under threat of the cudgel and a deadline, to capture and dispose of it. Many proclamations stand at the approaches to the ridge, ordering travelers to form companies and cross only during the three double-hours of the Snake, Horse, and Goat. During the six double-hours of the Tiger, Hare, Monkey, Cock, Dog, and Boar, no one is permitted to cross. Anyone traveling alone must wait for companions and cross in a group. It is already the end of the Goat hour and the beginning of the Monkey hour. Seeing you set off without even asking anyone, I knew you were throwing your life away for nothing. You would do better to rest here tonight. Tomorrow, take your time and wait until twenty or thirty people have gathered; then you can all cross the ridge together.” Hearing this, Wu Song laughed. “I am a native of Qinghe County and have crossed this Jingyang Ridge ten or twenty times at the least. When have I ever heard of a tiger here? Stop trying to frighten me with such damned nonsense. Even if there is a tiger, I am not afraid!” The innkeeper said, “I am trying to save you out of goodwill. If you do not believe me, come inside and read the authorities’ proclamation.” Wu Song said, “Shut your damned mouth! Even if there truly is a tiger, I am not afraid! You want to keep me lodging in your house so that in the dead of night you can murder me for my money and take my life; that is why you are frightening me with this damned tiger.” The innkeeper said, “Just listen to you! I act from nothing but goodwill, yet you take it for malice and repay me with words like these! If you will not believe me, then go your own way as you please!” Indeed:

p.src: It was already around the hour of shen, and the red sun was sinking languidly beside the hills. Spurred on by the wine, Wu Song pressed steadily up the ridge. Before he had gone much more than half a li, he saw a dilapidated temple to the mountain god. When he reached the temple, he saw an officially sealed notice pasted upon its gate. Wu Song stopped to read it. It said:

p.src: Proclamation of Yanggu County: A large tiger has recently appeared on Jingyang Ridge and taken human lives. The village headmen and hunters of every district have now been ordered, under penalty of the cudgel and within a fixed time, to hunt it down, but it has not yet been caught. All passing merchants and other travelers may cross the ridge in company during the three double hours of si, wu, and wei. At all other times, and for travelers alone, passage over the ridge is forbidden, lest lives be lost. Let all concerned take due notice.

p.src: Only after reading the sealed notice did Wu Song know for certain that there truly was a tiger. He was about to turn back to the tavern, but then thought, “If I go back, that fellow is sure to laugh at me and say I am no true man. I cannot turn back.” After pondering for a while, he said, “What the devil is there to fear? I will just go on and see what happens!”

p.src: As Wu Song walked on, the wine steadily rose in him. He slung his felt hat upon his back, tucked his quarterstaff beneath his ribs, and climbed the ridge step by step. When he looked back at the sun, it was gradually sinking from sight. It was the tenth month, when days were short and nights long, and evening came quickly. Wu Song said to himself, “What tiger could there possibly be? Men have merely frightened themselves and dare not climb the mountain.” Wu Song walked on for some distance; the wine took full effect, and he grew feverishly hot. Holding the quarterstaff in one hand and pulling open the front of his robe with the other, he staggered straight through a tangled grove. Seeing a broad, smooth slab of bluestone, he leaned the quarterstaff beside it, stretched himself out, and was just about to sleep when suddenly a fierce wind arose. The ancients composed four lines of verse describing that very wind:

p.src: Formless and shadowless, it pierces the breast; through all four seasons it blows all things into bloom. It snatches yellow leaves away from the trees, and entering the mountains drives white clouds forth.

p.src: It is said that in this world clouds attend the dragon and winds attend the tiger. As soon as that gust had passed, there came a tremendous thud behind the tangled trees, and out sprang a great tiger with glaring eyes and a white forehead. At the sight of it, Wu Song cried, “Ah!” He rolled down from the bluestone, seized his quarterstaff, and dodged beside the rock.

He rolled down from the bluestone, seized his quarterstaff, and dodged beside the rock.

p.src: The tiger was both hungry and thirsty. Pressing its two paws lightly against the ground, it hurled its whole body upward and came plunging down through the air. The shock startled all the wine out of Wu Song in a cold sweat. It happened faster than words can tell: as the tiger sprang, Wu Song gave a single sidestep and slipped behind it. A tiger has the greatest difficulty seeing behind itself, so it planted its forepaws on the ground and heaved its loins upward in a mighty toss. Wu Song merely ducked and dodged aside. When the tiger failed to toss him, it gave a roar like a thunderclap bursting in midheaven, so violent that the ridge itself shook; then, raising its iron-bar tail straight up, it lashed sideways with a single sweep. Once again Wu Song dodged aside. Now a tiger takes a man in only three ways: a pounce, a toss, and a sweep of the tail. If all three fail, half its fury is already spent. Having missed again with its tail, the tiger roared once more and wheeled around. Seeing the tiger turn back upon him, Wu Song swung the quarterstaff up in both hands and, putting all his lifelong strength into one blow, brought it cleaving down from overhead. There came a single crack, and branches and leaves showered rustling down before his face. Looking closely, he saw that the blow had missed the tiger. In his haste he had struck a dead tree squarely, snapping the quarterstaff in two and leaving only half of it in his hand.

p.src: The tiger roared, driven into a rage, turned, and sprang at him once more. Wu Song leapt aside again, retreating a full ten paces. The tiger landed with both forepaws directly before him. Wu Song flung the broken staff aside, seized the loose skin atop the tiger’s head with both hands, and bore it down with all his weight. The tiger struggled desperately, but Wu Song pinned it with all his strength and would not relax his grip in the slightest. With one foot he kicked wildly again and again at the tiger’s face and eyes. Roaring, the tiger clawed up two heaps of yellow earth beneath its body and dug itself a pit. Wu Song thrust the tiger’s muzzle straight down into the muddy pit. Tormented so by Wu Song, the tiger had little strength left. Keeping his left hand clamped tightly upon the skin atop its head, Wu Song freed his right hand, raised a fist as large as an iron hammer, and struck without cease with all the strength of his life. After fifty or seventy blows, fresh blood burst from the tiger’s eyes, mouth, nostrils, and ears. Exerting all his customary divine might and relying on the martial skill within him, Wu Song beat the tiger into a heap within half an hour, until it lay there like a brocade-covered sack blocking his way. An old-style ballad tells especially of Wu Song’s slaying of the tiger on Jingyang Ridge:

p.src: Wild winds rage over Jingyang Ridge; dark clouds for ten thousand miles veil the sunlight.

u.src: Wild winds rage over Jingyang Ridge; dark clouds for ten thousand miles veil the sunlight.

p.src: Before the eye, evening clouds hang screened by the woods; a piercing cold mist fills the vault of heaven.

u.src: Before the eye, evening clouds hang screened by the woods; a piercing cold mist fills the vault of heaven.

p.src: Suddenly a thunderous crash is heard, and from the mountainside flies forth the king of beasts.

p.src: Head held high, it bounds about displaying fang and claw, while deer and all their kind flee in frantic haste.

p.src: Seen close, it still seems possessed of a thousand-jun force; viewed from afar, its awe-inspiring might is gone on every side.

p.src: Its body lies across the wild grass, its brocade markings dimmed; both eyes are tightly shut and flash no more.

p.src: There on Jingyang Ridge, in less time than it takes to eat a meal, Wu Song’s flurry of fists and kicks had beaten the fierce tiger until it could no longer move, though breath still faintly panted from its mouth. Wu Song released it, went to the pine tree to find the broken end of his staff, and took it in hand. Fearing the tiger might not be dead, he beat it with the stump for another spell. The tiger had no breath left at all. Wu Song thought again, “Can I drag this dead tiger down the ridge from here? …”

p.src: He reached into the pool of blood and tried to lift it with both hands, but he could not move it. He had used up all his strength, and his hands and feet had gone limp. Wu Song returned to the bluestone and sat for a while, thinking, “It will soon be dark. If another tiger should spring out, how could I possibly fight it? I had better struggle down the ridge for now and come back tomorrow morning to deal with this.” He found his felt hat beside the stone, passed around the tangled grove, and painfully made his way down the ridge step by step.

p.src: He had gone scarcely half a li when two great tigers suddenly sprang from the withered grass. Wu Song cried, “Ah! This time I am done for!” Then the two tigers rose upright in the darkness. Wu Song peered at them and saw that they were two men wearing tiger skins sewn into garments and fitted tightly around their bodies. Each man held a five-pronged fork. Startled at the sight of Wu Song, they cried, “Have you eaten a man’s heart, a leopard’s liver, or a lion’s leg? Your whole body must be wrapped in sheer courage! How dare you cross the ridge alone at nightfall, unarmed? We cannot tell whether you are man or ghost!” Wu Song asked, “Who are you two?” One of them replied, “We are local hunters.” Wu Song asked, “What are you doing up on the ridge?” The two hunters exclaimed in astonishment, “You still do not know? There is now an enormous tiger on Jingyang Ridge that comes out every night and mauls people. Seven or eight of us hunters alone have already been lost. Countless travelers have also been eaten by the beast. The county magistrate has ordered the local headman and all of us hunters to capture it. But that accursed beast is so powerful that no one can approach it. Who dares go forward? Because of it, we have taken more strokes of the regulation cudgel than we can count, yet still cannot catch it. Tonight it is our turn again to hunt it. A dozen or so villagers are here with us, and we have set spring-bows and poisoned arrows all over the ridge to await it. We were lying in ambush here when we saw you striding boldly down from the ridge, and it gave us quite a fright. Who exactly are you? Did you see the tiger?” Wu Song replied, “I am from Qinghe County. My surname is Wu, and I am the second son. Just now, beside the tangled woods up on the ridge, I ran straight into that tiger and beat it to death with my fists and feet.” The two hunters stared at him in stupefaction and said, “Surely that cannot be true?” Wu Song said, “If you do not believe me, just look at the bloodstains still on my body.” The two asked, “How did you fight it?” Wu Song recounted once more the whole story of how he had fought the tiger. The two hunters were both amazed and delighted. They called the ten villagers over. The ten villagers, carrying steel forks, crossbows, swords, and spears, immediately gathered around. Wu Song asked, “Why did none of them follow you two up the mountain?” A hunter replied, “The beast is so fearsome—how would they dare come up?” The whole party of more than ten men now stood before him. The two hunters told the others that Wu Song had slain the tiger, but none of them would believe it. Wu Song said, “If you do not believe it, come with me and see for yourselves.” They all carried fire-steels and flints, so they quickly struck a flame and lit five or seven torches. They all followed Wu Song back up the ridge and saw the tiger lying there in a dead heap. They rejoiced greatly at the sight and first sent one man to report to the local headman and the leading household responsible for the matter. Meanwhile, five or seven of the villagers bound the tiger themselves and carried it down from the ridge.

p.src: When they reached the foot of the ridge, seventy or eighty people were already there, all surging forward in excitement. They carried the dead tiger at the head of the procession, seated Wu Song in a sedan chair, and bore him straight to the home of a leading local household. The householders and the local headman were waiting before the manor to welcome them. They carried the tiger into the thatched reception hall. Some twenty or thirty leading householders and hunters from the district came to see Wu Song. They asked, “Mighty warrior, what is your honored name? Where is your native place?” Wu Song replied, “I am from Qinghe County in the neighboring prefecture. My surname is Wu, my given name Song, and I am the second son. I was returning home from Cangzhou. Last night I became thoroughly drunk at the tavern on the far side of the ridge, and when I came up over it, I ran straight into this beast.” He then gave a detailed account of every move and blow with which he had fought the tiger. The leading householders declared, “You are truly a hero and a gallant man!” The hunters first brought game meat and drank cups of wine with Wu Song. Wu Song was exhausted from fighting the tiger and wished to sleep. The master of the house ordered his servants to prepare a guest room so Wu Song could rest for the time being. At daybreak, the leading householder first sent someone to report to the county seat; meanwhile, they jointly prepared a tiger bier, arranged everything properly, and made ready to escort it to the county offices. After dawn, Wu Song rose and washed. The leading householders had brought a whole sheep and a shoulder-pole load of wine and were waiting before the hall. Wu Song dressed, straightened his headcloth, and came out front to meet them. The leading householders offered him wine and said, “There is no telling how many lives this beast has taken, and because of it the hunters have suffered several rounds of the regulation cudgel. Today, through the good fortune of your arrival, this great scourge has been removed. First, the people of the district are blessed; second, travelers may pass safely—all this is truly your gift to us!” Wu Song thanked them, saying, “It was not through any ability of mine; I relied upon the good fortune and protection of you, my honored elders.” Everyone came forward to congratulate him. They ate and drank throughout the morning, then brought out the tiger and placed it on the tiger bier. The leading villagers all brought lengths of satin and ceremonial red silk to drape upon Wu Song. Wu Song left what little baggage he had in safekeeping at the manor. Then everyone went out before the manor gate together. The magistrate of Yanggu County had already sent men to receive Wu Song. After they had exchanged greetings, four manor servants were ordered to bring an open sedan chair and carry Wu Song. With the tiger carried in front and adorned with red silk and lengths of satin, they escorted Wu Song into Yanggu County.

p.src: When the people of Yanggu County heard that a mighty warrior had slain the tiger on Jingyang Ridge and was being escorted into town amid acclamation, they all came out to see, throwing the entire county seat into an uproar. Looking out from his chair, Wu Song saw people packed shoulder to shoulder and back to back, clamoring and jostling, filling every street and blocking every lane as they came to welcome the tiger. When they reached the gate of the county offices, the magistrate was already waiting especially for them in the hall. Wu Song descended from the chair, and the tiger was carried into the forecourt and laid upon the paved approach. The magistrate studied Wu Song’s imposing figure, then looked at the enormous, splendidly striped tiger and thought to himself, “If it were not a man like this, how could he possibly have killed such a ferocious tiger?” He then summoned Wu Song into the hall. Wu Song went before the hall and saluted. The magistrate asked, “You are the mighty warrior who killed the tiger. Tell me, how did you slay the beast?” Standing before the hall, Wu Song recounted the entire fight with the tiger. Everyone above and below the hall was struck dumb with amazement. The magistrate bestowed several cups of wine upon him there in the hall, then brought out a reward of one thousand strings of cash contributed by the leading households and gave it to Wu Song. Wu Song respectfully reported, “Through Your Honor’s good fortune and protection, I happened by sheer luck to kill this tiger. It was not through any ability of mine, so how could I dare accept the reward? I have heard that all these hunters were punished by Your Honor on account of this tiger. Why not distribute the thousand strings among them for their use?” The magistrate said, “Since that is your wish, mighty warrior, do as you please.” There in the hall, Wu Song distributed the reward money among all the hunters.

When they reached the gate of the county offices, the magistrate was already waiting especially for them in the hall.
Wu Song descended from the chair, and the tiger was carried into the forecourt and laid upon the paved approach.

The magistrate studied Wu Song’s imposing figure, then looked at the enormous, splendidly striped tiger and thought to himself, “If it were not a man like this, how could he possibly have killed such a ferocious tiger?”
He then summoned Wu Song into the hall.
Wu Song went before the hall and saluted. The magistrate asked, “You are the mighty warrior who killed the tiger. Tell me, how did you slay the beast?”
Standing before the hall, Wu Song recounted the entire fight with the tiger. Everyone above and below the hall was struck dumb with amazement.

ja: しょうきんいっせんかん
u.src: The magistrate bestowed several cups of wine upon him there in the hall, then brought out a reward of one thousand strings of cash contributed by the leading households and gave it to Wu Song.

Wu Song respectfully reported, “Through Your Honor’s good fortune and protection, I happened by sheer luck to kill this tiger. It was not through any ability of mine, so how could I dare accept the reward?
I have heard that all these hunters were punished by Your Honor on account of this tiger. Why not distribute the thousand strings among them for their use?”
The magistrate said, “Since that is your wish, mighty warrior, do as you please.”
There in the hall, Wu Song distributed the reward money among all the hunters.

p.src: Seeing that he was honest, generous, and virtuous, the magistrate wished to advance him and said, “Though you are originally a native of Qinghe County, it lies but a stone’s throw from our Yanggu County. What would you say if I appointed you today as a constable captain in this county?” Wu Song knelt and gave thanks, saying, “If Your Excellency is gracious enough to advance me, I shall remain indebted to you all my life.” The magistrate at once summoned his clerk to draw up the official papers, and that very day Wu Song was appointed captain of the foot constables. All the wealthy householders came to congratulate Wu Song on his good fortune, and for three or five days they feasted and drank without cease. Wu Song reflected, “I meant to return to Qinghe County to visit my elder brother, yet who would have thought that I should instead become a constable captain here in Yanggu County?” From then on, he enjoyed the magistrate’s favor, and his name became renowned throughout the countryside.

p.src: Another two or three days passed. One day, Wu Song went out before the county offices to stroll at his leisure when he heard someone behind him call, “Captain Wu, now that you have risen in the world, how can you neglect an old acquaintance like me?” Wu Song turned to look and cried, “Ah! What are you doing here?”

p.src: Had Wu Song not met this man, Yanggu County would never have been strewn with corpses and stained with blood. Where the steel blade rang, heads would roll; when the precious sword was swung, hot blood would flow. But who exactly was the man who called out to Captain Wu? Listen to the explanation in the next chapter.
